narrative: The model estimated a 35% probability that you would be a bad credit risk. That is not a majority, but it was above the bank’s approval cut-off, so the application was denied. The most influential signal was the short length of the credit you requested: nine months versus an approved-applicant average of about nineteen months. That shorter commitment worked in your favour, reducing the risk estimate. The second most important signal was your checking-account status. A negative balance below zero is uncommon among approved applicants—about 12.6% versus nearly 59% with no overdraft—so this counted against you and pushed the decision toward bad credit. The third most important signal was your employment type. Being in management, self-employed, or highly skilled is a relatively stable category and worked in your favour. Even so, the checking-account warning was serious enough that, together with the rest of your profile, the overall assessment still crossed the bank’s denial threshold. To improve your position, bring your checking account into a positive, stable balance and keep it there for several months; ask the bank what account status it would view as acceptable. If your account information is outdated or incorrect, provide corrected statements. Consider adding a guarantor or co-applicant if one is available, and reapply once your financial picture is stronger.
